The barred sorubim Pseudoplatystoma fasciatum is a large pimelodid catfish inhabiting the major river basins of South America. Field surveys indicate that newly emerged prolarvae, which hatch from demersal adhesive eggs, possess a wet weight at birth of only 0.0028 grams [Wwb = 0.0028 grams]. This minute size reflects the lecithotrophic phase during which the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves. Incubation under controlled conditions at 26 °C [T = 26 °C] results in an age at birth of 12 days [ab = 12 days], a duration consistent with the thermal dependence of embryonic development observed in other Neotropical siluriforms. The protracted incubation period, compared to many temperate catfishes, may be an adaptation to the relatively stable thermal regime of tropical lowland rivers. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva commences exogenous feeding after the yolk is largely absorbed, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth that continues through the postflexion and juvenile stages.

As juveniles grow, the allometric shift from larval to juvenile body plan is accompanied by a steep increase in body mass. The length-weight relationship typical of the species, derived from a large sample across its range, yields an ultimate wet weight of 12,000 grams [Wwi = 12,000 grams] for the largest adult specimens. This corresponds closely with the reported maximum standard length of 105 centimeters [Li = 105 centimeters] for the species, with the largest individuals likely representing long-lived females. The asymptotic mass is substantially greater than that of related congeners such as Pseudoplatystoma reticulatum, which rarely exceeds 8,000 grams in most river systems. Attaining such a large body size necessitates several years of sustained feeding on a piscivorous diet, primarily composed of migratory characiforms. Growth rates appear to be influenced by seasonal flood pulses, which enhance prey availability and create optimal conditions for rapid mass gain.

Reproductive maturation in the barred sorubim occurs at a total length of approximately 45 centimeters [Lp = approximately 45 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 909 grams [Wwp = 909 grams] according to the established length-weight regression. These values indicate that individuals become capable of gametogenesis and first spawning at a relatively modest fraction of their ultimate size, roughly 45 percent of the maximum standard length. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from wild-caught specimens confirms that vitellogenesis is initiated once this threshold is crossed, with oocyte development proceeding synchronously within each ovary. The onset of reproductive maturity coincides with the seasonal appearance of mature gonads during the rising-water period, suggesting that environmental cues, such as photoperiod and river discharge, play a crucial role in triggering the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Spawning migrations upstream are a well-documented behavior during this phase.

Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for the barred sorubim is 4,015 days [am = 4,015 days], equivalent to approximately 11 years. This longevity estimate, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated through otolith microchemistry analysis, positions the species among the longer-lived pimelodids. For catfish of this size class, the age-based mortality schedule appears to be relatively low, with adult survivorship exceeding 80 percent annually in pristine habitats. The maximum lifespan is likely constrained by the energetic demands of repeated spawning events and by the physiological costs of maintaining a large somatic mass in a seasonally fluctuating environment. Individuals nearing the end of their natural lifespan exhibit reduced feeding activity and diminished gonadal output, consistent with reproductive senescence.

The maximum daily reproductive output of this species, based on observations of Pseudoplatystoma corruscans under optimal thermal conditions at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], involves females producing approximately 63,853 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 63,853 eggs per spawning event] and spawning roughly once per year [F_R_i = spawning roughly once per year]. Characterized by high fecundity and group-synchronous oocyte development, the barred sorubim exhibits a reproductive strategy that compensates for high larval mortality through massive initial offspring numbers. Fecundity estimates from gravid females collected during the flood season show that larger individuals contribute disproportionately to the spawning stock, with total egg production scaling positively with body size. The timing of the reproductive cycle is tightly linked to the annual flood pulse, ensuring that larvae encounter optimal conditions for growth and survival in the newly inundated floodplain habitats. River regulation through dam construction poses a significant threat to this strategy.
